title: Managing an options position
teaches: You get out of an option with the opposite trade; set the target, the stop (on the stock's chart or the option's price) and a re-check date before you buy; take profits in full or in part; treat a roll as a close plus a new trade that costs or pays real money; and deal with short options before expiry, because only a buy-to-close ends assignment risk.

walkthroughs.title: Getting out is a trade
steps: You get out of an option the way you got in: with a trade, this time on the other side.
If you bought it, sell to close. If you sold it, buy to close.
Most option positions end that way, not by exercise.
Until you close, a profit is only on paper.

walkthroughs.title: Write the exit before the entry
steps: Before you buy, set two exits: the target where you take profit and the stop where you're wrong.
Your stop can sit on the stock's chart or on the option's price. The Options Industry Council calls that your choice.
Add a date to re-check the trade. Time decay is gradual at first and speeds up near expiry.

walkthroughs.title: A roll is two trades
steps: A roll closes your option and opens a new one at another strike, another expiry, or both.
The old option's gain or loss is settled when it closes. The roll doesn't erase it.
The new option is a fresh trade. It needs a reason of its own.

questions.q: You own a call and want to be fully out of the trade, with no shares. Which order does that?
questions.why: Sell to close. You opened by buying, so you exit with a closing sale of the same contract. FINRA calls this doing the reverse. Exercising would buy the shares instead. A put is a different contract, so buying one closes nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Bought to open, sell to close. To get out, you make the opposite trade.

wrong.Buy to close: You bought this call, so a buy is the wrong side. The closing trade for it is a sale.
wrong.Exercise the call: Exercising a call buys the shares. That's the opposite of having no shares.
wrong.Buy a matching put: A put is a different contract, so it closes nothing. You would hold the call and a put, not be out.

questions.simple: Sell to close, because you bought the call to open, and the opposite trade ends it with no shares left.

reasons: stable definition from FINRA and the Options Industry Council, both Tier 1

questions.q: In options, what does it mean to roll a position?
choices: Close it and open a new one
questions.answer: Close it and open a new one
questions.why: Close it and open a new one. The Options Industry Council defines a roll as closing an open option and opening a new one. The new one has a different strike, a different expiry, or both. The two legs are usually done at the same time. It is not exercise, adding size or moving a stop.
questions.lesson_line: A roll is two trades in one ticket: a close and a new open.

wrong.Exercise it early: Exercise turns the option into stock. A roll trades out of one option and into another.
wrong.Add contracts as it drops: That's averaging down on the same option. A roll replaces the option.
wrong.Widen your stop: That's widening your stop. A roll changes the contract itself: strike, expiry or both.

questions.simple: Rolling means you close the option you hold and open a new one, at another strike, another expiry, or both.

reasons: stable definition, Tier 1 glossary plus an agreeing Tier 2 source

questions.q: On an option trade, a date can be an exit trigger, not just a price.
questions.why: True. The Options Industry Council says some buyers set price targets or re-evaluation dates. Fidelity calls this a time exit: it caps how long you stay in. When it hits, you at least re-check the trade. It does not mean you must sell on that date.
questions.lesson_line: Options run on a clock. Give every trade a date to re-check, as well as a stop.
questions.simple: True, because some option buyers set a date to check the trade again, not just a price target.

reasons: key is only that a date CAN be a trigger; Tier 1 and Tier 2 agree

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: You sold a put. To get out of it, you ___ to close.
questions.why: Buy. FINRA says an investor who sold an option exits with a closing purchase. The Options Industry Council's glossary agrees: a purchase closes a short option, and a sale closes a long one. So selling would not close this put. A roll closes it but opens a new one, so you'd still be in.
questions.lesson_line: Sold to open, buy to close. Bought to open, sell to close.
questions.simple: Buy, because a put you sold is closed by buying the same contract back.

reasons: stable definition from FINRA and the Options Industry Council

questions.q: You own a call and want a stop-loss order on it. Which is true?
choices: You pick its trigger: stock or option
Most exchanges don't accept option stops
Only the option's price can trigger it
Once hit, it must become a limit order
questions.answer: You pick its trigger: stock or option
questions.why: You pick its trigger: the stock or the option. The Options Industry Council calls that a matter of personal preference. Most exchanges allow stop-loss orders on options, but check that your broker accepts them. Once triggered, the stop becomes a market or a limit order. For us, the premium paid is the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop on an option can key off the stock or the option. Check that your broker takes it.

wrong.Most exchanges don't accept option stops: It's the reverse. The Options Industry Council says most exchanges allow stop-loss orders on options. Check that your broker accepts them.
wrong.Only the option's price can trigger it: The stock can be the trigger too. E*TRADE's contingent order closes an option when the stock hits a price you set.
wrong.Once hit, it must become a limit order: It can be either. Once triggered, a stop on an option becomes a market order or a limit order.

questions.simple: You choose, because the trigger can be the stock's price or the option's price, as you prefer.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook B25 (options: the premium paid is the stop)
question re-asked 2026-11-12 to remove a both-of-the-above tell

questions.q: In options, what does rolling out mean?
questions.why: Moving to a later expiry. Rolling out closes the option and opens the same position in a later expiration cycle. tastylive says rolling out always adds time; it is also called rolling forward. Moving to a higher strike is rolling up. Moving to a lower strike is rolling down.
questions.lesson_line: Out means later. Up and down mean the strike.

wrong.Moving to a higher strike: That's rolling up. Rolling out changes the expiry.
wrong.Closing the trade for good: A roll closes one option and opens another, so you're still in the trade.
wrong.Adding more contracts: That's adding size. A roll swaps the contract, not the count.

questions.simple: Rolling out means moving to a later expiry, because out is about time, while up and down are about the strike.

reasons: stable definition, two Tier 2 publishers agree plus the Tier 1 glossary

questions.q: When should you decide where you'll take profit and where you'll cut the loss?
questions.why: Before you buy the option. Fidelity says it can help to have an exit plan even before you enter. E*TRADE adds that a plan made in advance is less likely to be swayed by emotion. Once a trade is open, emotions and loss aversion get in the way. You can still re-check the plan later, but you write it first.
questions.lesson_line: Write the target and the stop before the order. Then follow them.

wrong.Once it shows a profit: Then you're deciding with a profit in front of you. Emotions and loss aversion get in the way.
wrong.When expiry gets close: By then time decay is speeding up against you. Plan the exit before you enter, not near the end.
wrong.After it moves against you: That's when loss aversion makes it hardest to act. Set the stop while you're calm.

questions.simple: Before you buy the option, because a plan made while you are calm is less likely to be swayed by emotion.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Rolling a losing option out to a later expiry erases the loss on the first one.
questions.why: False. A roll closes the first option and opens a new one. Investopedia says the gain or loss on the original contract is settled. tastylive says rolling a loser locks in the losing trade. The new option is a separate trade with its own risk.
questions.lesson_line: A roll books the loss. It doesn't hide it.
questions.simple: False, because the roll closes the first option, so its loss is booked there. The new option is a separate trade.

reasons: Tier 1 glossary plus two agreeing Tier 2 publishers

questions.q: You bought 6 calls at $1.80. They double to $3.60, and you sell 3. How much cash comes back?
questions.why: $1,080. Three contracts at $3.60, times 100 shares, is $1,080. That matches what all 6 cost at $1.80, since half as many at twice the price is the same money. So if the 3 you kept go to zero, the trade breaks even, fees aside. An option buyer can't lose more than the premium paid.
questions.lesson_line: Sell half at a double and your cost is back. The worst case on the rest is zero.
questions.simple: $1,080 comes back, because 3 contracts at $3.60 times 100 equals what all 6 cost you at the start.

deeper.example: Say the stock reverses and the 3 calls you kept fall to zero. You took in $1,080 on the 3 you sold, which is what all 6 cost. The trade ends at break-even before fees. Had you held all 6 and they fell to zero, you would have lost everything you paid.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (lesson line, 2026-11-09)

wrong.$540: Sells the 3 at the old $1.80 price.
wrong.$2,160: Counts all 6 contracts. You sold only 3.
wrong.$10.80: Forgets that one contract covers 100 shares.

questions.story: Your call is bid $4.00. You set a sell trailing stop $1.50 under the bid. The bid climbs to $6.20, then starts to fall.
questions.q: At what price does your trailing stop trigger?
questions.why: $4.70. A sell trailing stop sits $1.50 under the highest bid. It started at $2.50 and rose as the bid climbed. From the $6.20 high it sits at $4.70, and it never moves lower. When the bid falls through it, it becomes a market order.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop follows a winner up and never steps back down.

wrong.$2.50: That was the starting stop. It moved up as the bid rose.
wrong.$4.00: That's where the bid was when you set it. The stop trails the high, not your start.
wrong.$6.20: That's the high. The stop sits the trail amount under it.

questions.simple: $4.70, because the stop trails the $6.20 high by $1.50 and never moves back down.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: E*TRADE says some traders close an option at a 50% loss. On a call bought for $3.20, at what option price do they exit?
questions.why: $1.60, half of $3.20. E*TRADE says some traders close if they double their money or lose 50%. That is a plan some traders use, not our rule. For us, the premium paid is the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Cutting at half is a plan some traders use. Our rule for options: the premium paid is the stop.
questions.simple: $1.60, because a 50% loss on a $3.20 call leaves it worth half that price.

reasons: computed key
touches the owner's rulebook B25 (options: the premium paid is the stop); reveal now states the house rule
fixed before (question text, 2026-11-09)

wrong.$4.80: Adds 50 percent instead of taking it off.
wrong.$6.40: That is the double-your-money exit, not the 50% loss exit.
wrong.$2.70: Takes 50 cents off instead of 50 percent.

questions.story: You own 4 calls you bought at $2.50. They're $4.10 now, with a month left. You think the stock has more room, but you want to lock in part of the gain.
questions.q: Which move fits that view?
questions.why: Sell 2 and let 2 ride. The Options Industry Council covers this exact view. If the stock has further to go but you want less invested, sell a portion. The calls you keep still carry the risk of a reversal. Exercising would throw away time value and need cash for the shares.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength, keep some for the run.

wrong.Hold all 4 for now: That lets the whole gain ride, with the full risk of a reversal. It locks in nothing.
wrong.Buy 4 more now: That doubles your contracts at a higher price. It adds risk instead of locking in the gain.
wrong.Exercise 2, keep 2: Exercising throws away the time value left and needs cash for the shares. The gain then rides in the stock.

questions.simple: Sell 2 and let 2 ride, because selling part locks in some gain while the rest stays in for more upside.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A11 (sell some into strength), consistent with it
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Your 50 call is worth $7.00. You sell it and buy the 55 call for $3.50. How much cash comes back, per contract?
questions.why: $350. You sell the 50 call for $7.00 and buy the 55 call for $3.50. The difference, times 100 shares, is cash back in your account. The Options Industry Council calls this buying a more distant strike for a credit. You stay in the move with less money on the table, but the premium on the new call can still be lost.
questions.lesson_line: Rolling a winner up takes cash off the table and keeps you in the move.
questions.simple: $350 comes back, because you take in $7.00 and pay $3.50 for the higher strike, times 100 shares.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$3.50: Forgets that one contract covers 100 shares.
wrong.$1,050: Adds the two prices instead of taking the difference.
wrong.$700: Counts only the cash from selling the 50 call.

questions.q: If you buy back a short call during the day, it can't be assigned to you that night.
questions.why: True. OCC processes closing buys before exercises, and assignment goes by your net position after each day's close. A short call you bought back is gone by then, so it can't be assigned. One caveat: check with your broker that it wasn't assigned already.
questions.lesson_line: When in doubt, close them out. A short option you've bought back can't be assigned.
questions.simple: True, because a short call you bought back during the day is no longer open, and only open positions can be assigned.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-09 checker added f90)

questions.story: You sold a call spread. The stock rallied through your short strike, so you roll the spread up to higher strikes and out a month.
questions.q: What did the roll do to your assignment risk?
choices: Reduced it, but didn't remove it
Removed it, the strike is higher now
Raised it somewhat, as it runs longer
Moved it onto your long call instead
questions.answer: Reduced it, but didn't remove it
questions.why: Reduced it, but didn't remove it. The Options Industry Council says rolling reduces assignment risk on American-style options but does not entirely remove it. The new short call has a higher strike and more time, so assignment is less likely. Only buying back the short call ends the risk.
questions.lesson_line: A roll moves a short option's risk. Only a buy-to-close ends it.

wrong.Removed it, the strike is higher now: You're still short a call after the roll. As long as a short option stays open, it can be assigned.
wrong.Raised it somewhat, as it runs longer: Assignment risk grows deeper in the money and as expiry nears. A higher strike and more time cut it.
wrong.Moved it onto your long call instead: A long option can't be assigned. You decide whether to exercise it.

questions.simple: Reduced but not removed, because you are still short a call after the roll, and an open short option can be assigned.

reasons: Tier 1 source states this exact case (OIC April 2026 FAQ)

questions.q: Your call expiring Friday is bid $0.90. The same strike two months out costs $3.10. What does rolling out cost, per contract?
questions.why: $220. You sell the expiring call at the $0.90 bid and buy the later one for $3.10. The difference, times 100 shares, is $220 you pay. More time means more time value, so the later expiry costs more. That $220 is new money at risk, and it can be lost.
questions.lesson_line: Rolling a long option out isn't free. Every month you add is paid for, and it can be lost.
questions.simple: $220, because you get $0.90 for the old call and pay $3.10 for the new one, times 100 shares.

deeper.counter: A roll out can feel like keeping the same trade alive. It is not. You booked $0.90 on the old call and paid $3.10 for a new one. If the stock still does not move, time decay works on the new call too. It starts slowly, then speeds up near expiry, and the premium you paid is what you can lose.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$400: Adds the two prices. You sell one call and buy the other.
wrong.$310: Counts only the new call and forgets the $0.90 you get back.
wrong.$2.20: Forgets that one contract covers 100 shares.

questions.q: You sold a put spread for $1.20. It costs $0.25 to close now. Hold to expiry instead: what's the most extra you can make per spread?
questions.why: $25. On a credit spread, the $1.20 credit is the most you can make. Closing now costs $0.25, so holding can add at most that $0.25 a share, times 100. For that $25, you keep the spread's full risk until expiry. tastylive makes the same point about a short option near max profit.
questions.lesson_line: Near max profit, a short spread pays little to hold and keeps all its risk.
questions.simple: $25 is the most extra, because only the $0.25 it costs to close is left to earn, times 100.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$120: Thinks you can still make the whole credit. Most of it is already made.
wrong.$95: Gives what closing now already earns, not what is left to make.
wrong.$145: Adds the 0.25 closing cost to the 1.20 credit.

questions.story: It's expiry day. Your short put is in the money, and you'd rather roll it out a month than take the shares.
questions.q: How do you work the roll?
choices: Well before the close, as one order
Close now, sell the new put later
Wait for the final minutes to roll
Let it expire, then sell a new put
questions.answer: Well before the close, as one order
questions.why: Well before the close, as one order. A roll's close and new open are usually done together, to cut slippage if the stock moves in between. Schwab says liquidity can dry up near the close on expiry day, and spreads may widen. So for a roll, sooner may be better.
questions.lesson_line: Roll well before the close on expiry day, in one order. Don't leave it to the bell.

wrong.Close now, sell the new put later: That splits the roll into two trades, and the stock can move in between. A roll is usually done in one step.
wrong.Let it expire, then sell a new put: In the money, it will most likely be assigned, and you get the shares you wanted to avoid.
wrong.Wait for the final minutes to roll: That's when liquidity can dry up and spreads may widen. Schwab says sooner may be better.

questions.simple: Roll well before the close in one order, because liquidity can thin and spreads widen late on expiry day.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting to see if the put finishes out of the money. In the final minutes, liquidity can dry up and spreads may widen. An in-the-money option is generally exercised at expiry. So the short put is likely assigned, and you get the shares you meant to avoid.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook E57 (market orders: the limit was dropped from the key) and A6 (options only as a defined-risk alternative)
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.story: Your call is down 60% with a week left. The stock broke the level your plan was built on. A friend says roll it out three months.
questions.q: What would that roll really be?
choices: Taking the loss, then a new bet
A patient way to wait out the dip
A free extension of the call
Just more time on the same trade
questions.answer: Taking the loss, then a new bet
questions.why: Taking the loss, then a new bet. The roll closes the old call, so its loss is settled right there. tastylive says rolling a loser locks in the losing trade and opens a new one. The later call also costs more, because more time means more time value. Here the setup already broke, so the new bet starts on a failed idea.
questions.lesson_line: If the setup broke, I close it. Rolling a broken idea is just buying it again.

wrong.A free extension of the call: The later call has more time value, so it costs more. You pay for those extra months.
wrong.Just more time on the same trade: The old call is closed and its loss booked. The new call is a separate trade at today's price.
wrong.A patient way to wait out the dip: The level your plan was built on broke. tastylive calls a rolled loser a new low probability trade.

questions.simple: Taking the loss and a new bet, because the roll closes the old call before it opens a new one.

deeper.trap: Rolling out feels like patience. But the old call is closed at a loss, and the money for the new call is fresh risk. The new call is a fresh trade and needs a reason of its own. Your plan's reason, the level the stock broke, is gone. Without a new reason, closing beats rolling.

reasons: fixed before (distractor replaced 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Being listed on an exchange means an option has a market to close in.
questions.why: False. The options disclosure document says there is no guarantee a market will exist for every option at all times. Schwab adds that a liquid market is not guaranteed. Option prices can also stop tracking the stock the way you expect. So check the bid and the spread before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Check the bid and the spread before you buy. An exit you can't fill isn't an exit.
questions.simple: False, because there is no promise that a market to sell in will exist for every option at all times.

deeper.trap: An option can look profitable on paper and still be hard to sell. FINRA says profits aren't guaranteed until a closing trade is done. The disclosure document says a market may not exist for every option at all times. So the time to check the bid and the spread is before you buy, not when you need out.

reasons: fixed before (why split, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: The options network tastylive sells options for a credit. It says it usually rolls a short option 7 to 21 days before expiry.
questions.q: What is it trying to avoid?
questions.why: Gamma and assignment risk. tastylive names both as its reason for rolling early. The Options Industry Council backs each one. Gamma rises sharply in at-the-money options as time is removed. Assignment risk grows as expiration approaches. Faster time decay near expiry helps a seller, so it is not the threat.
questions.lesson_line: Near expiry, a short option near the money can swing fast. Decide early whether to close or roll.

wrong.A drop in implied volatility: Falling volatility tends to lower option prices. That helps a seller, so it isn't what they're running from.
wrong.Time decay slowing down: Decay speeds up near expiry, which helps a seller. The danger is how fast the price can swing.
wrong.The stock sitting still: Short options gain when the stock sits still. Their risk is a sharp, sudden move.

questions.simple: Gamma and assignment risk, because near expiry a short option near the money can swing fast and is likelier to be assigned.

deeper.trap: Fast decay in the last weeks looks like free money for a seller. The same weeks bring a sharp rise in gamma for at-the-money options, so a small stock move can swing the option hard. tastylive's 7 to 21 days is its own practice, not a rule. The point is to decide early whether to close or roll.

reasons: story carries tastylive's own 7 to 21 day practice, which can change
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Holding a big winner to expiry is free, since a call can't lose more than its premium.
questions.why: False. An option holder can't lose more than the premium paid, but that cap is on your cost, not your gain. FINRA says profits aren't guaranteed until you close the trade. Letting a winner ride means taking the risk of a reversal. A big open gain can shrink all the way back.
questions.lesson_line: The premium caps the loss. Nothing caps how much open profit you can give back.
questions.simple: False, because the premium caps your loss on what you paid, not the open profit you can give back.

deeper.trap: Traders mix up two caps. The premium caps what you can lose of your own money. Nothing caps how much open profit you can hand back. A call that is well up is a paper gain until you sell it, and a reversal can take all of it. Holding to expiry risks the gain, not just the cost.

reasons: Tier 1 sources (OIC, FINRA) agree

questions.story: You own calls with a stop-loss order on the option at $2.00. Bad news hits, and the bid drops straight to $1.40.
questions.q: Your stop turns into a market order. Where does it most likely sell?
questions.why: Near $1.40, at the bid. Once triggered, the stop is a market sell order, and a market sell fills at the best bid. Schwab warns the fill can be well under the stop price. A stop-limit would avoid that, but it might not fill at all. A stop sets when you get out, not the price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop picks when you get out, not the price. In a fast market, expect the bid.

wrong.At $2.00, your stop price: The stop is a trigger, not a promised price. Once it fires, it takes the bid.
wrong.Not until $2.00 trades again: That's how a stop-limit behaves. It can leave you holding while the price keeps falling.
wrong.At the ask, just above $1.40: A market sell order fills at the best bid, not the ask. The Options Industry Council says so directly.

questions.simple: Near $1.40, because a triggered stop is a market sell order, and that sells at the best bid there is.

deeper.trap: Many traders think a stop guarantees its price. It doesn't. Here the bid dropped straight from above $2.00 to $1.40, so the market order took about $1.40. A stop-limit at $2.00 would not fill until $2.00 traded again, which may not happen while the price keeps falling.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook B25 (premium paid is the stop) and D41 (real stop orders)

questions.story: Your calls are up 150% with three weeks left. The stock just hit the target your plan set for its whole move.
questions.q: What do you do?
questions.why: Take the profit, close it. The Options Industry Council covers this case. If the stock made most or all of its expected move, you might close and take the profit. Your plan set that target when you were calm. Holding for more is a new plan made on the fly, with the risk of a reversal. With three weeks left, time decay is also speeding up.
questions.lesson_line: When the stock hits the target you set, take it. You made that call when you were calm.

wrong.Hold for more, it's working: That's a new plan made on the fly. Letting it ride means taking the risk of a reversal.
wrong.Roll up and add contracts: Adding contracts adds risk just as your plan says the move is done.
wrong.Exercise and keep the shares: Exercising throws away the time value left, and it needs cash for the shares.

questions.simple: Take the profit and close, because the stock already made the move your plan expected, so the reason to hold is gone.

deeper.trap: A 150% gain makes it feel like the trade is still working, so why stop? But the reason you bought is used up: the stock hit the target for its whole move. Anything more is a new bet with your profit at stake. It is made in the rush of a win, not with the calm plan.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook A11 and E51 (trims and a trail, for shares)
fixed before (question text, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: You sold a put for $0.80. tastylive says it closes a losing short option at a net loss of twice the credit.
questions.q: Under that rule, at what price do you buy the put back?
questions.why: $2.40. On a short option, your loss is the buy-back price minus the credit you took in. A loss of twice the $0.80 credit is $1.60. So you buy back at $0.80 plus $1.60, which is three times the credit. tastylive's own example works the same way: collect $1.00, close at $3.00.
questions.lesson_line: On a short option, the loss is buy-back minus credit. Do that math before you sell.

wrong.$1.60: That's twice the credit as a price. Buying back there loses only one times the credit.
wrong.$0.80: That's where you sold it. Buying back there is break-even, not a stop.
wrong.$0.40: Cuts the credit in half instead of tripling it.

questions.simple: $2.40, because a loss of twice the $0.80 credit means paying back the credit plus twice it, three times $0.80.

deeper.trap: The common slip is to buy back at twice the credit, $1.60. That price loses only one times the credit. The rule counts the net loss, not the option's price. It is tastylive's practice, and tastylive says only that it found this can be optimal. It is not a UCT rule.

reasons: computed key on tastylive's own rule, a practice that can change
touches the owner's rulebook A6 and B25 (options only as a defined-risk alternative)

questions.q: For UCT, what is the stop on an option you buy?
choices: The premium you paid for it
Half of the premium you paid
A level on the stock's chart
No stop, options need no rules
questions.answer: The premium you paid for it
questions.why: The premium you paid. Our rulebook sets no further rules for options: the premium paid is the stop. A buyer can't lose more than the premium paid. So that premium is the most the trade can cost.
questions.lesson_line: For us, an option's stop is the premium paid. A buyer can't lose more than that.

wrong.Half of the premium you paid: Some traders cut at a 50% loss, E*TRADE says. Our rule doesn't: the premium paid is the stop.
wrong.A level on the stock's chart: The Options Industry Council leaves the trigger to you. Our rulebook has chosen: the premium paid is the stop.
wrong.No stop, options need no rules: Our rulebook sets no further rules, but it does name the stop: the premium paid.

questions.simple: The premium you paid, because our rule says the premium paid is the stop on an option.

reasons: house rule B25, quoted from the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9)

questions.q: In our rulebook, options are a defined-risk alternative to shares, used only occasionally.
questions.why: True. Our rulebook says to trade shares, and that options are only a defined-risk alternative. It adds that we use options occasionally, with no further rules.
questions.lesson_line: We trade shares. Options are an occasional, defined-risk alternative.
questions.simple: True, because our rulebook says we trade shares and use options only now and then, with set risk.

reasons: house rules A6 and B25, quoted from the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9)

conflicts: The '21-day rule' in the unit plan: the version usually repeated ('manage short options at 21 days to expiry') is credited to tastytrade's research, but the tastylive page that could be fetched (s22) says it rolls '7-21 days prior to expiration'. No day count is keyed as a rule: q21 gives tastylive's own 7-21 practice as a given and keys only the reason, which OIC (Tier 1) states on its own (gamma rises sharply as time is removed, f37; assignment risk grows as expiration approaches, f28; decay accelerates in the last three weeks, f35).

Profit and loss percentages and multiples: E*TRADE's example exits at double or at a 50% loss (f65); tastylive closes short-premium winners at 50% of max profit (s21, not quoted as a fact) and says closing a loser at a net loss of 2x the credit 'can be optimal' (f88). Per the unit plan, no percentage or multiple is keyed as UCT's rule or as best practice. q11 states the member's own plan ('out if it loses half its value') and names E*TRADE's example only in the reveal; q25 gives tastylive's 2x rule in the story as tastylive's and keys only the arithmetic (a loss of twice the credit means buying back at three times it), which tastylive's own $1.00 / $3.00 example states (f89); q17 computes from given prices and cites tastylive only for the risk/reward point (f70). tastylive's 'optimal' claim rests on its own back-tests and is not repeated.

OIC's long call page says some buyers set price targets or re-evaluation dates while 'others play it by ear' (f02). q07 ('decide the exit before you buy') is keyed on Fidelity (f50) and E*TRADE (f60, f61), two Tier 2 publishers that agree; OIC is not cited as saying a plan is required, and q03 keys only that a date CAN be an exit trigger (OIC f02 plus Fidelity's time exit, f77).

Trailing stops on options: E*TRADE's example trails the option's bid by a fixed dollar amount (f78); Schwab's trailing-stop page (f80, f81) is written for stocks. Both say a sell trailing stop only moves up and becomes a market order when triggered. q10 keys only that mechanic (calc: high minus trail); whether a given broker trails the bid, the last trade or the mark is not keyed.

What triggers a stop order on an option (a trade, or the bid or offer) has differed by exchange and over time in Cboe's rule filings. The file never keys the trigger mechanics; q23 says only that a stop that has turned into a market sell order fills at the best bid (OIC, f21) and can fill well under the stop (Schwab, f58).

Investopedia's roll-up example (s20) reads 'either selling the June call option or by simultaneously buying' a September call; the roll it then describes is a sell and a buy together. q13's key rests on OIC's FAQ (f18, Tier 1: sell the options, then buy a more distant strike for a credit); the Investopedia line (f67) is cited only for 'protecting part of the profits'.

Schwab's 'When Should I Roll My Options Trades?' (November 25, 2025) is a video with no page text and is not cited. Fidelity's 'Rolling covered calls' (written by The Options Institute at Cboe) was read but is about covered calls (F6.13's ground) and is not cited.

Expiry-day times (Schwab's 3 p.m. CT trading cut-off, OCC's exercise thresholds and deadlines) change with products and rules and belong to F6.16. f53 is quoted for its point that liquidity thins near the close; no question asks for a time.
Every dollar figure ignores commissions and fees, as OIC's own examples do ('less commission, of course').
